title: The Challenge: Small-Group Instruction is NOT a Time of Day
author: Ben Zulauf
summary: Zulauf, a former instructional coach, uses his own past advocacy for an 80-minute literacy block built around daily small-group rotations to indict a structure that roughly 90% of teachers still use. The research he cites (Sorensen and Hallinan 1986; Amendum et al. 2009; Connor, Morrison, and Petrella 2004) finds no achievement benefit from small-group instruction when the fair comparison is made, which is 20 minutes of small-group time against the same minutes a teacher could spend with the whole class. Worse, the students assigned to lower-ability groups tend to receive fewer learning opportunities, less teacher support, and more of the unsupervised seatwork that only benefits already-proficient readers. Group placements themselves are often compromised by assessment noise, behavior, race, language, and SES rather than true instructional need, which means the very students the structure is meant to help are the ones it tends to widen the gap for. The honest verdict is that daily small-group rotations feel responsive and look like differentiation, but the evidence suggests they are more likely to increase the achievement gap than close it, so small groups should be a tool used sparingly, not a time of day.
points: The fair research comparison for classroom teachers is 20 minutes of small-group instruction against 80 minutes of whole-group instruction (because rotations force a tradeoff), and under that comparison small groups do not outperform.

Students in the lowest-ability groups spend the most time in small-group instruction yet get fewer opportunities to learn, less teacher support, and lower eventual test scores, which widens rather than narrows the gap.
Group placements are frequently inaccurate, driven not just by assessment but by behavior, race, language proficiency, and SES, undermining the differentiation rationale.
Seatwork that fills the non-teacher minutes of a rotating literacy block helps already-proficient readers and hurts the less secure, inverting the intended equity purpose.
Small-group instruction should be treated as a targeted tool, not a structural daily block, despite roughly 90% of teachers using it as such (Scholastic Research and Validation, 2024).
quotes: The apparent result is that there is no effect of grouping on individual reading achievement" (Sorensen and Hallinan, 1986, p. 532). The researchers go on to say that "students in grouped classes are exposed to fewer opportunities for learning than students in ungrouped classes" (p. 534), so while learning is intensified, they simply have fewer chances to learn.

Perhaps the fewer opportunities to learn result from the teacher working more with the students who need the most support. I certainly made the recommendation to meet with the less secure students more frequently than those who were already proficient. Considering this, proponents of small-group instruction might say that small-group time is beneficial to help struggling readers catch up; however, this study also found "that more opportunities for learning exist in the high group than in lower level groups" (p. 539).

Every aspect of this construct benefits our readers who are already proficient. I largely supported this practice so that teachers could provide reteaching to our struggling readers. I wanted to create a time for them to catch up. And this is why using the research is so incredibly important. Relying a gut feeling or intuition or vibes led to me endorsing a practice that's largely ineffective.

Daily small-group rotations may make us feel good. In the moment, we may feel that we're doing a better job of addressing individual student needs, but the research suggests that this approach may be more likely to increase the achievement gap rather than reduce it. This is a huge issue considering that evidence suggests that about 90% of teachers use this structure (Scholastic Research and Validation, 2024).

I understand that we cannot entirely eliminate small-group instruction. It is a necessary evil. But it should be treated as a tool rather than a time of day, and when it's used, there are things we can do to make this time more effective.” Archived from Challenge Accepted (Substack) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
